items.title: When does the move work?
items.prose: The proof for $\sqrt2$ used: if $n$ divides $p^2$, then $n$ divides $p$. For $n = 4$ it failed at $p = 6$.
items.question: For which $n$ does $n \mid p^2$ give $n \mid p$ for every integer $p$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You trusted an odd number. $9 \mid 3^2$, but $9 \nmid 3$.
You missed the square factor 4. $12 \mid 6^2 = 36$, but $12 \nmid 6$.
You missed the square factor 4. $8 \mid 4^2 = 16$, but $8 \nmid 4$.

feedback.correct: Right. 3 is prime, and 6 is two primes, each passed on to $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try small $p$, and split each $n$ into primes.

explain.text: A prime that divides $p \cdot p$ divides $p$, so $n = 3$ works. For $n = 6$, $2 \mid p$ and $3 \mid p$ give $6 \mid p$. A square factor breaks it: $p = 3$ for 9, $p = 4$ for 8, $p = 6$ for 12.

items.title: Supremum and infimum
items.prose: Let $E = \{(-1)^n (1 - \tfrac1n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. The first terms are $0, \tfrac12, -\tfrac23, \tfrac34, -\tfrac45, \tfrac56$.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\sup E = 1$, and no term equals it.
$\inf E = -1$, and no term equals it.

options.why: You stopped at $n = 2$. $\tfrac34$ and $\tfrac56$ are larger even terms.
You looked only at $n = 1$. The odd terms $-\tfrac23, -\tfrac45, \dots$ are below 0.
You took the last listed even term. $n = 8$ gives $\tfrac78$, larger still.

feedback.correct: Right. Even terms climb to 1, odd terms fall to $-1$, and neither limit is reached.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the terms by the parity of $n$.

explain.text: Even terms are $1 - \tfrac1n$, below 1 and within any $\varepsilon$ of it. Odd terms are $-(1 - \tfrac1n)$, above $-1$ and within any $\varepsilon$ of it. So $\sup E = 1$, $\inf E = -1$, and neither is attained.

items.title: Small enough
items.prose: The Archimedean property gives some $n$ with $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. Odd denominators work too.
items.question: What is the smallest $n$ with $\tfrac{1}{2n + 1} < 0.004$?

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{2n+1} < 0.004$ means $2n + 1 > 250$, so $n > 124.5$. The smallest whole number is 125. Check: $\tfrac{1}{251} \approx 0.003984$.

items.title: A fraction between
items.prose: Run the density recipe for $a = -0.3$, $b = -0.29$: the smallest whole $n > \tfrac{1}{b - a}$, then $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$.
items.question: Fill in $n$ and $m$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $b - a = 0.01$, so start from $\tfrac{1}{0.01} = 100$.

byKey.r0c1: For $n$: $\tfrac{1}{0.01} = 100$, and $n$ must be strictly greater, so 101.
byKey.r1c1: For $m$: $101 \times (-0.3) = -30.3$. The floor rounds down, to $-31$, and adding 1 gives $-30$.

explain.text: $n = 101$ and $na = -30.3$. The floor rounds down, to $-31$, so $m = -30$. Check: $-0.3 < \tfrac{-30}{101} \approx -0.29703 < -0.29$.

items.title: A place in the walk
items.prose: The walk lists positive fractions diagonal by diagonal, $p + q = 2, 3, \dots$, top row first, skipping any not in lowest terms. $\tfrac15$ is 10th.
items.question: What position does $\tfrac34$ take?

feedback.correct: Right. Diagonal 7 runs $\tfrac16, \tfrac25, \tfrac34$ in places 12 to 14.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count lowest-terms fractions diagonal by diagonal.

byKey.repeats: You counted repeats such as $\tfrac22$ and $\tfrac24$. The walk skips them.
byKey.diag: You started diagonal 7 one place late. Diagonals 2 to 6 fill places 1 to 11.

explain.text: Diagonals 2 to 6 hold $1 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 11$ fractions. Diagonal 7 begins $\tfrac16, \tfrac25, \tfrac34$, all in lowest terms. So $\tfrac34$ is 14th.

items.title: What the rationals lack
items.question: Which property does $\mathbb{R}$ have and $\mathbb{Q}$ lack?

options.text: Every non-empty subset bounded above has a least upper bound in the set.
Between any two different numbers lies another.
options.why: You chose density. The average of two rationals is rational, so $\mathbb{Q}$ has it too.

options.text: Every number has a larger whole number.
options.why: You chose the Archimedean property. It holds in $\mathbb{Q}$ as well.

options.text: The sum of two numbers is in the set.
options.why: You chose closure under addition. Sums of fractions are fractions.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the property that $\{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 2\}$ breaks inside $\mathbb{Q}$.

explain.text: $\{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 2\}$ is bounded above but has no least rational upper bound. So $\mathbb{Q}$ is not complete. Density, the Archimedean property and closure hold in both.

items.title: Bisection for the root of 5
items.prose: Bisect $[2, 3]$ for $\sqrt5$: square the midpoint, and keep the half whose ends square to either side of 5.
items.question: What is the left end of the interval after 3 halvings?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $2.5^2$, $2.25^2$ and $2.125^2$ with 5 in turn.

byKey.right: You gave the right end. After three steps the interval is $[\tfrac{17}{8}, \tfrac94]$.
byKey.two: You stopped after two steps. Step 3: $2.125^2 = 4.515625 < 5$, so the left end moves up.

items.title: The diagonal on the whole numbers
items.prose: A classmate runs the diagonal argument on the whole numbers, written as digit strings $1, 2, 3, \dots$ padded with leading 0s. The new number differs from the $k$th in its $k$th digit from the right.
items.question: Why does this not show that $\mathbb{N}$ is uncountable?

options.text: The new digit string has infinitely many nonzero digits, so it is not a whole number at all.
It does show that: $\mathbb{N}$ is uncountable.
options.why: You accepted the conclusion. $\mathbb{N}$ is listed by $f(n) = n$, so it is countable.

options.text: Whole numbers may end in a run of 9s.
options.why: You reused the two-names problem. A whole number has only one digit string.
You blamed the list. It holds every whole number; the new string is what fails.

feedback.correct: Right. The diagonal escapes the set, so nothing is contradicted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the diagonal object is in $\mathbb{N}$.

explain.text: With the 5 and 4 rule, every digit of the new string is 4 or 5. A whole number has only finitely many nonzero digits. So the diagonal object is not in $\mathbb{N}$, and its absence from the list proves nothing.

items.title: An infimum proved
items.prose: Prove that $\inf\{\tfrac1n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$ with the two-part test for an infimum. One line is flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Part one: every $\tfrac1n > 0$, so 0 is a lower bound.
By the Archimedean property, choose $n$ with $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$.
Then $\tfrac1n < 0 + \varepsilon$, so no number above 0 is a lower bound.

lines.why: You put 0 in the set. No $n$ gives $\tfrac1n = 0$; the infimum is not attained.

feedback.correct: Right. A lower bound, and nothing above it is one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lower bound first, then any $\varepsilon$, then a term below $0 + \varepsilon$.

byKey.d1: You used the line putting 0 in the set. $\tfrac1n > 0$ for every $n$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: This mirrors the proof that $\sup\{1 - \tfrac1n\} = 1$. Part one: 0 is below every term. Part two: for any $\varepsilon$, the term $\tfrac1n$ with $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$ is below $\varepsilon$.
